summary: Conveys the Internet Activities Board's recommendations for developing network management standards for the TCP/IP environment, in the short and long term. It does not define an official protocol, but reflects IAB policy on further work.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1052 records how the Internet Activities Board (IAB) wanted network-management work to proceed in 1988. It recommends a short-term protocol, a longer-term framework and shared data definitions.

subtitle: The 1988 IAB plan for short-term and long-term network management work.

tldr.problem: Several network-management efforts were progressing, creating a risk that the Internet community would build incompatible tools.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB recommended SNMP as a short-term basis, ISO CMIS/CMIP for longer-term work, IETF responsibility for SNMP, and a shared extended MIB.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1052 records IAB policy and committee recommendations; its text explicitly says it does not define or propose an official Internet Protocol.

today: RFC 1052 is an April 1988 memo that says it does not define or propose an official Internet Protocol. The supplied metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: The IAB's Decision
sections.content:
At its March 1988 meeting, the IAB reviewed an ad hoc committee report and endorsed its recommendations. It directed the IETF chair to form working groups for network-management information and short-term SNMP extensions.

The MIB group's definitions were to be supplied to both the SNMP and CMIS/CMIP groups. The memo says this was intended to keep the items monitored by the two frameworks compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: The board accepted the committee's plan and asked the Internet Engineering Task Force to organize the work. One group would define shared management data, and another would address short-term needs.

sections.title: Short-Term and Long-Term Choices
sections.content:
The IAB recommended Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) as the basis for network management in the short term. It urged the SNMP group to keep the protocol simple, consider needed extensions and publish results within 90 days.

For longer-term work, the IAB recommended developing and testing the ISO Common Management Information Services and Protocol (CMIS/CMIP) for TCP/IP. The committee also called for an extended Management Information Base (MIB) usable by the short- and long-term approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: The board chose a simple protocol for immediate needs and an ISO framework for longer-term work. It wanted both approaches to use the same descriptions of managed data.

sections.title: The Competing Management Efforts
sections.content:
The committee compared HEMS, SGMP and ISO CMIS/CMIP. HEMS had a broad management information base and an experimental implementation; SGMP had implementations in use and was comparatively simple; CMIS/CMIP had extensive documentation but little implementation.

The committee noted that all three efforts used ASN.1 for data structures, but their management information differed in scope and detail. It recommended focusing community effort on one short-term and one long-term direction.
sections.plainLanguage: The committee compared three approaches with different levels of implementation, scope and detail. It recommended coordinating their work rather than allowing incompatible management tools to develop separately.

sections.title: The Four Committee Recommendations
sections.content:
The ad hoc committee recommended adapting SNMP for immediate use, developing CMIS/CMIP for longer-term use, assigning the SNMP effort to an IETF task force, and defining an extended MIB as a high priority.

The committee report says Craig Partridge offered to withdraw HEMS from consideration if that helped produce Internet-wide agreement. The IAB memo records these recommendations as policy direction, not as a protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The committee recommended a near-term protocol, a later framework, oversight by the Internet Engineering Task Force and shared management data. These were work directions, not protocol rules.
